lines.text: The stock exchange is where shares in publicly listed companies are bought and sold, and understanding its vocabulary opens a window into global finance and economics. The London Stock Exchange (LSE), founded in 1801, is one of the world's oldest and most influential. The FTSE 100 index tracks the 100 largest companies listed on the LSE by market capitalisation — names like Shell, HSBC, and Unilever. When a company goes public through an IPO (Initial Public Offering), it sells shares to investors for the first time. Share prices fluctuate based on supply and demand, company performance, economic conditions, and investor sentiment. A bull market describes rising prices and optimism; a bear market signals falling prices and pessimism. Traders buy shares hoping prices will rise (going long) or bet against companies expecting prices to fall (short selling). Dividends are portions of company profits distributed to shareholders, typically quarterly. Key financial metrics include earnings per share (EPS), price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), and market capitalisation. Trading floors, once bustling with shouting traders, have largely been replaced by electronic trading systems. Brokers execute trades on behalf of clients, charging commissions or fees. The stock market serves as both an economic indicator and a wealth-creation mechanism — pension funds, endowments, and individual investors all participate. Crashes, corrections, and rallies create headline news and affect millions of people's retirement savings and financial security.

lines.text: FTSE is pronounced 'Footsie', not spelt out. It stands for Financial Times Stock Exchange. 'The Footsie is up 50 points' is typical news language. The FTSE 100 (large companies) and FTSE 250 (mid-sized) are the most-followed indices.
